A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same HyperVQ work and support comparison of the text, equations, tables and figures. v1 ends with references; v2 additionally contains Appendix A, which was included in the comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original reconstruction, generation, classification, clustering, corruption-robustness and ablation results on CIFAR-100, ImageNet, MNIST and ImageNet-C.

after.justification: v2 retains the original vision experiments and adds LibriSpeech pretraining results and an original synthetic codeword-assignment experiment in Appendix A.6.

M1.justification: The core procedure remains exponential projection, unidirectional hyperbolic MLR, Gumbel selection with straight-through gradients, and hyperplane-representative codewords mapped back to Euclidean space. The rewritten equations and explicit objective-computation step clarify existing operations; the speech experiment applies the same quantizer.

E1.justification: Section 5.5 adds speech self-supervised pretraining on LibriSpeech 960h, substantially extending the previously vision-only empirical coverage. Appendix A.6 additionally evaluates synthetic Euclidean, uniform Poincare-ball and boundary-concentrated populations. Existing vision datasets and tasks are retained.

E2.justification: The corresponding vision comparisons retain their baseline membership, including the original ablation variants. The new speech comparison evaluates unmodified wav2vec 2.0 against its HyperVQ-equipped counterpart in Figure 6, adding a comparison system without broadening the existing vision baseline suite.

E3.justification: v2 introduces masked contrastive speech pretraining evaluated through validation loss and codebook perplexity. Appendix A.6 adds a distinct assignment protocol with N=100,000, K=25, perturbed grid centers versus hyperplanes, and uniform versus boundary sampling. These are new evaluation designs; the stated budgets and configurations of retained vision experiments remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix A.6 and Figure 7 add a focused toy analysis examining codeword-assignment balance under different geometries, initializations and sampling distributions. The existing component ablations, MNIST clustering/noise analysis and ImageNet-C robustness evaluation are retained.

E5.justification: v2 Tables 1, 3 and 6 add ± values to reconstruction errors, classification accuracies and ablation results previously reported as point values. Their statistical meaning and estimation procedure are unspecified, and no repeated-run or seed counts are added. The existing Inception Score uncertainty values are unchanged.

E6.justification: The existing vision central values and rankings are unchanged, including HyperVQ's 31.59% CIFAR-100 accuracy at K=512 and ImageNet FID of 130.31. Figure 6 adds higher speech codebook usage and lower validation contrastive loss for HyperVQ; Figure 7 adds assignment histograms showing more balanced usage in the illustrated hyperbolic settings.

T1.justification: v2 adds volume-scaling arguments, codebook-usage and partition-probability definitions, and Appendix A's Chernoff-based underutilization argument under idealized sampling. This substantially extends v1's background mathematics. Section 3.1.2 also corrects the Poincare-ball radius description and adds the missing curvature factor to the conformal metric.

C1.justification: Although v1 already reported better codebook usage, v2 makes codebook collapse a central problem and explicitly claims that hyperbolic volume growth mitigates it. This substantially reframes the abstract, introduction and contributions while retaining the original claims about disentanglement and discriminative performance with comparable generative quality.

C2.justification: v2 adds a substantive self-balancing explanation linking negative curvature to more uniform partitions and reduced collapse, while acknowledging that learned encoder outputs need not satisfy idealized sampling assumptions. It also interprets the speech results as improved learning dynamics and broader applicability. The existing low-precision instability limitation remains.

D1.justification: v2 explicitly identifies reconstruction evaluation splits, expands Gumbel-sampling details and documents synthetic initialization and sampling. Conversely, v1's explicit safe-projection equation becomes only a general radius-cap mention, and its explicit VQVAE MSE-training statement disappears. Most architecture details are relocated; hardware, optimizer and implementation-library disclosures remain.

R1.justification: v2 adds Chernoff (1952) for the new concentration argument and explicitly motivates hyperbolic geometry relative to spherical, mixed-curvature and SPD alternatives. The existing related-work coverage and basic novelty positioning are otherwise retained; citation-format changes do not constitute new research coverage.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, VQVAE preliminaries and method exposition are substantially rewritten around codebook collapse. Architecture descriptions move into the experimental sections, subsection organization changes, and a broader-impact statement and Appendix A are added.

P2.justification: v2 substantially reformats the document, merges v1's accuracy and perplexity Tables 3–4 into Table 3, and removes the classification-pipeline diagram. It revises the MNIST visualization to display quantized vectors and adds the speech learning curves and synthetic assignment plots as Figures 6–7.

improvement.justification: The new speech evidence strengthens the previously asserted cross-domain applicability, and corrected geometric definitions improve accuracy. However, Appendix A's central inference from volume growth to balanced normalized assignment probabilities is asserted rather than established; its toy comparison also changes initialization and sampling. Undefined uncertainty values and reduced projection detail further limit the reporting gains. These benefits and weaknesses leave the net quality change uncertain.
